identity: Arabic financial newswire brief on oil prices - a headline plus four body paragraphs from a pan-Arab/Gulf economics desk: crude falling back below the 70-dollar level, the US savings rate at a 15-year high per Commerce Department data, the S&P 500 and Dow moves on Wall Street, and Wednesday's US Energy Department inventory build. Agency register: third person, no dialogue, no quotation, heavy nominalisation, stacked PP and relative-clause tails. Doctrine section K (news compendium) for behaviour, section B/L for prose rhythm. Nothing here is narrative, classical, hadith or memoir, so none of the inverting registers (section H) apply.
law: The gold is punctuation-derived, not semantics-derived: reconstruct the ink. Boundaries are (a) the full stop ending each newswire sentence, (b) the comma that sets off a fronted cohesive adjunct or a trailing attribution, and (c) every ASCII period the guardless splitter saw - which in this document includes the decimal points inside 0.2, 0.2 and 0.4. Target sentence ~12-20 tokens (expository band). LAW 1 applies at full strength (waw + a fresh finite clause carrying a NEW argument = cut), and LAW 4 blocks the two long tails (a subordinate clause that FOLLOWS its main clause - ba'da an, allati, allathi - belongs to it).
reasoning: Register calibration first, per LAW 6. Agency financial copy, expository band, 154 real tokens, so I expect roughly 10-13 segments. Batch-1 base rate (LAW 0) says my failure mode in exactly this kind of text is leaving 25-35 token blobs, so I pushed density up rather than trusting my instinct for periodic prose. FREE SITES: 6, 51, 77 and 123 sit immediately before an <NL>, and 158 is the final token; taken unconditionally - the pre-<NL> boundary was 100 percent correct across 18 docs in batch 1. HEADLINE (0-6): 'asaar al-naft tataraaja' an mustawa 70 dulaaran' is a complete verbal sentence with a finite verb, not the verbless NP-plus-predicate caption shape that K3 splits (the 'aynawi batalan li-ka's al-imarat' case), so no internal colon-split. No boundary inside it. THE DECIMALS - the single biggest call in this document. Tokens 90/91, 114/115 and 122/123 read '0 2', '0 2', '0 4'. These are 0.2 percent, 0.2 percent and 0.4 percent with the marks stripped: a 0.2 percent weekly slide in crude, the S&P down 0.2 and the Dow down 0.4 are textbook daily figures, and the surrounding 'bi-hawali' and the two tatweel-stranded 'bi-' prepositions confirm the reading. Decisively, the tokenizer SPLIT each pair, so some punctuation character stood between those digits, and the only candidate is the decimal point. Doctrine A1/A2 records that this pipeline has no guards of any kind - it split 'Robert L. Rothstein', it split 'hindawi.org' into 'hindawi || org', it split 'sad.ba' into 'sad || ba'. A splitter carrying no abbreviation guard and no URL guard carries no digit guard either, so it split 0.2 as well; the digit-pair guard is the commonest heuristic in sentence splitters and this one demonstrably has none. Checklist item 3 from batch 1 names digits explicitly and records that these reconstructed dots cost me 5 free boundaries in a single colophon. So I cut at 90, 114 and 122. Coherence check in favour: all three sites yield the identical shape (0 || 2 ||, 0 || 2 ||, 0 || 4 ||) rather than three ad-hoc decisions. Risk accepted knowingly - if the theory is wrong I take 3 cheap false cuts, if right I recover 3 expensive misses, and LAW 0 prices a false cut at about one fifth of a miss. @20 'dulaaran' / before 'wa-dhalika': CUT. Structurally this is C4 - waw plus a new topic NP (dhalika) plus a nominal predicate PP - and the source near-certainly carried a comma. Argued against by K5, where 'wa-huna' welded and cost me a false cut, since 'wa-dhalika' is likewise an anaphoric cohesive opener that adds no new referent and could never follow a period without leaving a fragment. The decider is length: without this cut the lead paragraph runs 8-46, thirty-nine tokens, which is precisely the 25-plus blob LAW 0 says I habitually leave. Cut, med. @25 'al-usbu'' / before 'ba'da an': NO CUT. LAW 4 is explicit and names ba'da an: a subordinate clause that FOLLOWS its main clause belongs to it. This is exactly the error I made at doc_56781db1019f @634, where I read a trailing ba'da an as fronting the next clause; I will not repeat it on a guess about a comma. This leaves segment 21-46 at twenty-six tokens, which I accept as law-protected length rather than override written law. @42 'malmus' / before 'ma'a imkaniyyat': NO CUT, rejected after argument. B5 tempts here (a comma-set parenthetical becomes two boundaries, not zero), but the two ma'a-PPs are not a list - the second narrows the first - and a comma before a bare ma'a-PP is not an Arabic press habit. @46 'al-inkimash' / before 'khassatan': CUT, and the lowest-confidence boundary in the document. The ground is purely orthographic: 'khassatan' is comma-magnetic in Arabic journalism. It rides entirely on the 'a comma often became a boundary' pathway - the same pathway as @20, so the two are correlated rather than independent. @20 has independent structural support and @46 has none, hence lo. @63 before 'li-tasila' and @107 before 'li-yankhafida': NO CUT. Both are lam-plus-subjunctive result clauses welded to their heads; a purposive lam is never a clause break. @72 ''aaman' / before 'wafqan': CUT. Trap avoided first - 'wafqan' is a single word whose waw is root-internal, NOT a coordinator, so LAW 1 has nothing to say here and this is not a waw-clause cut. It is the attribution comma: '... mundhu nahwa 15 'aaman, wafqan li-bayanat wizarat al-tijara al-amrikiyya.' is near-universal press pointing, and J3 makes a trailing source attribution its own segment. Splits paragraph 2 into 20 plus 5, both in band. @91 '2' / before 'wa-fi bursat wall street': CUT, my highest-confidence non-free boundary. Full LAW 1 - waw, a fronted locative, a new subject (mu'ashshir standard and bawrz 500) and its own verb (sajjala). Every argument is new. @115 '2' / before 'kama': CUT. J7 records 'kama' opening a segment (doc_70d28c9dfebb @152), and a comma before kama in a two-index comparison is standard pointing. PARAGRAPH 4 (125-158) - my main residual risk, argued at length. Thirty-four tokens with no internal boundary, well over the 12-20 band, and LAW 0 screams at me here. But every candidate site is barred by LAW 4: @133 before 'ithra' is a bare causal preposition with no comma habit at all; @139 before 'allati' and @150 before 'allathi' are relative clauses, and LAW 4 names allathi in its blocked set. Arabic newswire closers routinely stack two relatives into a single long period, which is what this is. I chose to obey my own written law over the base-rate prior, on the principle that overriding graded law on a hunch is worse than a possible miss. Flagged for the doctrine: @150 ('al-suq al-amriki' before 'allathi yu'addu akbar suq') is the one site I would revisit first if this document grades badly, since a non-restrictive appositive gloss is the one place a comma could plausibly have fired against LAW 4. NEGATIVE SCAN completed for reconstructed dots: no Latin script anywhere in this document; 70, 70, 15, 500 and 4 are bare integers with no dot; 'al' at 18 and 'bi' at 113 and 121 are article and preposition stranded by a stripped tatweel, not by a sentence mark, so no cut there; 'aand' at 99 is a spelled-out Arabic transliteration of 'and', not an ampersand; 'bawrz' carries a stripped apostrophe, not a period. FINAL DENSITY: 13 segments over 154 real tokens, mean 11.8, or 15.5 ignoring the three one-token decimal fragments - squarely in the expository band and comfortably denser than my batch-1 bias.
